Appendix B
Constraints on interpretation imposed by discrete integrals

In this Appendix, we consider in what ways the semantics of the ZX and ZH calculi are constrained, simply by choosing to define them in terms of discrete integrals on a finite set
{\mathbf{D}}
, but without fixing a specific measure
\mu
for those integrals beyond requiring
\mu(\{x\})
to be the same for all
x\in{\mathbf{D}}
.
We also consider how choosing a different presentation from Eqn. (
20
) for the discrete Fourier transform would impact the measure
\mu
.

In order to limit the scope of this exploration, we limit ourselves to
Ockhamic
semantic maps of ZX and ZH calculi.
This is a constraint on semantic maps which was introduced for the case
{\mathbf{D}}=\{0,1\}
in Ref.
[
19
, pp. 31 & 34]
, and which we extend to arbitrary sets
{\mathbf{D}}=\{L,L{+}1,\ldots,U{-}1,U\}
below.

B.1
Ockhamic interpretations of ZX and ZH diagrams

The semantics of ZX and ZH nodes (
e.g.
, as in the original articles
[
1
,
30
]
defining them) are conventionally chosen to be (about) as simple as possible when expressed via summation notation.
However, as Ref.
[
19
]
noted, there may be practical advantages to considering alternative interpretations of those generators, in the form of simplified rewrite systems.
This raises the question of what a reasonable ‘search space’ of semantic maps may be for these calculi, for the purpose of denoting multilinear operators over
{\mathcal{H}}
for a fixed vector space
{\mathcal{H}}\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{D}
(as opposed for instance to
equivalence classes
of such operators).

In Ref.
[
19
]
, one of us mooted sets of constraints on semantic maps
{[\mspace{-2.75mu}[\smash{\,\cdot\,}]\mspace{-2.75mu}]}
for ZX- and ZH-diagrams, which is flexible enough to represent a range of possible semantics for the generators without a proliferation of parameters for the dots and boxes.
Those definitions were proposed to guide investigation into semantics for ZX- and ZH-diagrams on qubits, which is a special case which enjoys several special properties which do not readily extend to the general case
D>1
in general, and which therefore may have been overspecialised in some ways.
We propose the following revision of the definitions of
[
19
, pp. 31 & 34]
for
D>1
in general, letting
{\mathbf{D}}=\{L,L\,{+}\,1,\ldots,U\,{-}\,1,U\}
for integers such that
U-L+1=D
.
14
14

14

One way in which these definitions revise those of Ref.
[
19
, pp. 31 & 34]
is in allowing an amplitude different from
1
, for the
\left|0\right\rangle^{\otimes n}\!\left\langle 0\right|^{\otimes m}
component of green dots, for the
\left|\smash{\omega^{0}}\right\rangle^{\otimes n}\!\left\langle\smash{\omega^{0}}\right|^{\otimes m}
component of red dots, and the components
\left|y\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|
of H-boxes for which none of the entries
x_{1},\ldots,x_{m},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}
are zero.
Given the introduction of functions
{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
to represent amplitudes, this seems to us a mild extension.

•

A semantic map
{[\mspace{-2.75mu}[\smash{\,\cdot\,}]\mspace{-2.75mu}]}
of
ZX diagrams
in terms of operators
{\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes m}\to{\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes n}
for arbitrary
m,n\in{\mathbb{N}}
, is
Ockhamic
if it satisfies Eqn. (
5
), and if there exists a sequence
(u_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}}
of positive scalars such that
u_{2}=1
,
15
15

15

The constraint
u_{2}=1
was not present in the original proposed definitions of ‘Ockhamic’ semantic maps for ZX or ZH diagrams in Ref.
[
19
, pp. 31 & 34]
.
We propose this revised definition so that red and green phase-free
1\to 1
dots, and the white and gray
1\to 1
dots, would all represent unitary transformations.
This constraint is satisfied in practise for all existing Ockhamic semantic maps for ZX and ZH diagrams.

and so that the following equations are satisfied for functions
\Theta:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
​:

\displaystyle{}{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZX-green-phase-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\,u_{m{\!\!\;+}n}\sum_{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}\!\!\;\Theta(x)\;\left|x\right\rangle^{\!\otimes n}\!\left\langle x\right|^{\!\!\;\otimes m}\!,

\displaystyle{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZX-red-phase-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\,u_{m{\!\!\;+}n}\sum_{k\in{\mathbf{D}}}\!\!\;\Theta(k)\,\left|\smash{\omega^{-k}}\right\rangle^{\!\otimes n}\!\left\langle\smash{\!\>\omega^{k}\!\;}\right|^{\!\!\;\otimes m}\!,

\displaystyle{\Bigl[\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigl[\,\smash{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZX-H-plus-box.pdf}\end{gathered}$}}\,\Bigr]\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigr]}\;\!

\displaystyle=\;\!\text{\small$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{D}}$}\mathop{\sum\sum}_{x,k\in{\mathbf{D}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi ikx/D}\left|k\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|,

\displaystyle{\Bigl[\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigl[\,\smash{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZX-H-minus-box.pdf}\end{gathered}$}}\,\Bigr]\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigr]}\;\!

\displaystyle=\;\!\text{\small$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{D}}$}\mathop{\sum\sum}_{x,k\in{\mathbf{D}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi ikx/D}\left|k\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|.

We propose this definition in the interest of having a calculus in which the green dots and the red dots being are related by the two kinds of Hadamard boxes, which in turn relate to the quantum Fourier transform; but also retaining the ‘Only the Connectivity Matters’
[
1
,
13
]
property.
16
16

16

It may prove to be preferable, after all, to retain the notational convention seen in most existing presentations of ZX-based calculi
[
8
,
12
,
23
,
41
]
of having red dots be related to green dots via conjugation by the Fourier transform.
One might describe such an interpretation as a ‘conjugate-Ockhamic’ interpretation (or, elect to redefine ‘Ockhamicity’ to favour the interpretation in which this conjugation relation holds).

•

A semantic map
{[\mspace{-2.75mu}[\smash{\,\cdot\,}]\mspace{-2.75mu}]}
of
ZH diagrams
in terms of operators
{\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes m}\to{\mathcal{H}}^{\otimes n}
for arbitrary
m,n\in{\mathbb{N}}
, is
Ockhamic
if it satisfies Eqn. (
5
), and if there exist sequences
(u_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}}
,
(h_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}}
, and
(g_{k})_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}}
of positive scalars such that
u_{2}=1
,
15

h_{0}=1
, and so that the following equations are satisfied for
c\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
and for functions
\mathrm{A}:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
:

\displaystyle{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-H-phase-box-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}\,

\displaystyle=\;h_{m{+}n}\!\mathop{\;\sum\sum\;}_{\mathclap{{x\in{\mathbf{D}}^{m}\!,\,y\in{\mathbf{D}}^{n}}}}\mathrm{A}(x_{1}\!\cdot\!\cdot\!\cdot x_{m}y_{1}\!\cdot\!\cdot\!\cdot y_{n})\!\left|y\right\rangle\!\!\left\langle x\right|

\displaystyle{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-gray-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\;g_{m{+}n}\!\mathop{\;\sum\sum\;}_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{m}\!\!\>,}\,{y\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{n}}\\[1.50694pt]
\sum\limits_{h}x_{h}+\sum\limits_{k}y_{k}\;\!\equiv\,0\end{subarray}}}\,\left|y\right\rangle\!\!\left\langle x\right|

\displaystyle{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-white-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=u_{m{+}n}\!\sum_{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}\!\left|x\right\rangle^{\!\otimes n}\!\left\langle x\right|^{\!\!\;\otimes m},

\displaystyle{\Bigl[\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigl[\,\smash{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-gen-not-dot.pdf}\end{gathered}$}}\,\Bigr]\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigr]}

\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}\left|-c{-}x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|\;.

We propose this definition in the interest of emphasising the theme of semantics involving simple constraints on classical indices, having the generalised-not dots represent simple permutations of the standard basis,
17
17

17

Our attitude is flexible as to whether
c
-not-dots should denote the transformation
\left|x\right\rangle\mapsto\left|-c{-}x\right\rangle
as we define it here, or instead
\left|x\right\rangle\mapsto\left|c{-}x\right\rangle
.
These two conventions lead to slightly different rewrite systems, either of which may be considered favourable depending on other conventions one might adopt to simplify notation.
We would in fact prefer the latter convention of representing
\left|x\right\rangle\mapsto\left|c{-}x\right\rangle
, were it not for the impact on the relationship with ZX red dots, the ZX stabiliser phase notation, and the notation for the Pauli operators.
A clever notational convention might possibly resolve these issues.

having degree-0 H-boxes with parameter
\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}
(taken as short-hand for a function
t\mapsto\alpha^{t}
) stand directly for scalar factors of
\alpha
, and retaining flexsymmetry of the interpretation of the generators.

As in Ref.
[
19
]
, these two conditions of ‘Ockhamicity’ (for ZX- and for ZH-diagrams) are proposed as an interpretation of the design principles and features of the ZX- and ZH-calculi
[
1
,
30
]
, but does not necessarily represent some unifying property of these two different families of diagrams.
18
18

18

Indeed, if one identifies an H-box with degree
2
and amplitude parameter
\omega={\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i/D}\in{\mathbb{C}}
in the ZH calculus, with the Hadamard plus box of ZX diagrams, this imposes significant constraints on the parameters
h_{2}
,
g_{k}
, and
u_{k}
.

We may consider how the constraint of using an ‘Ockhamic’ semantic map, for ZX diagrams and for ZH diagrams, interacts with the constraint of imposing a simple semantics for these diagrams via discrete integrals.
Specifically, we determine what constraints are imposed on the parameter
\nu
governing the measure
\mu
, and on the scalar factors in Eqns. (
78
) and (
79
), by considering Ockhamic semantic maps on the ZX and ZH generators for which Eqns. (
28
) and (
29
) hold.

B.2
Ockhamic semantics for ZH diagrams

Consider what constraints are imposed on an Ockhamic semantic map of ZH diagrams, by requiring Eqns. (
29
) to hold.
(These will in fact be less restrictive in a sense than the comparable constraints for semantics of ZX diagrams, owing to the explicit role in Eqn. (
78
) for the quantum Fourier transform.)

We proceed directly by considering how the expressions in Eqn. (
79
) may be expressed as integrals with respect to the measure
\mu
, and then considering the consequences of requiring Eqns. (
29
) to hold.
Note in particular how, for a multi-coefficient vector
x\in{\mathbf{D}}^{m}
, we have
\left|x\right\rangle=\left|x_{1}\right\rangle{\otimes}\left|x_{2}\right\rangle{\otimes}\cdots{\otimes}\left|x_{m}\right\rangle=\nu^{m}{\left|\left.\!\!\>x_{1}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\!\>\otimes\!\>}{\left|\left.\!\!\>x_{2}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\!\>\otimes\!\>}\cdots{\!\>\otimes\!\>}{\left|\left.\!\!\>x_{m}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}=\nu^{m}{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}
.
Similarly, for every sum over
x\in{\mathbf{D}}^{m}
that we turn into an integral, we introduce a factor of
\nu^{-2m}
(one factor of
\nu^{-2}
for each coefficient
x_{j}\in{\mathbf{D}}
).
We then have:

\displaystyle{}{\Bigl[\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigl[\,\smash{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-gen-not-dot.pdf}\end{gathered}$}}\,\Bigr]\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigr]}\,

\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}\!\left|-c{-}x\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|\;=\;\nu^{2}\!\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}\!{\left|\left.\!\!\>-c{-}x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}\;=\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}}{\left|\left.\!\!\>-c{-}x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}\;,

\displaystyle{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-white-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\;u_{m{+}n}\!\sum_{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}\!\left|x\right\rangle^{\!\otimes n}\!\left\langle x\right|^{\!\!\;\otimes m}

\displaystyle=\;u_{m{+}n}\cdot\nu^{m{+}n}\!\sum_{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}\!{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}^{\!\otimes n}\!{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}^{\!\!\;\otimes m}

\displaystyle=\;u_{m{+}n}\cdot\nu^{m{+}n{-}2}\!\!\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}^{\!\otimes n}\!{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}^{\!\!\;\otimes m}\;,

(80c)

\displaystyle{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-H-phase-box-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\,h_{m{+}n}\cdot\nu^{m{+}n}\!\mathop{\;\sum\sum\;}_{\mathclap{{x\in{\mathbf{D}}^{m},y\in{\mathbf{D}}^{n}}}}\mathrm{A}(x_{1}\!\cdot\!\cdot\!\cdot x_{m}y_{1}\!\cdot\!\cdot\!\cdot y_{n})\;{\left|\left.\!\!\>y\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}

\displaystyle=\,h_{m{+}n}\!\cdot\nu^{-(m{+}n)}\mathop{\int\!\!\!\!\int}_{\mathclap{{x\in{\mathbf{D}}^{m},y\in{\mathbf{D}}^{n}}}}\!\mathrm{A}(x_{1}\!\cdot\!\cdot\!\cdot x_{m}y_{1}\!\cdot\!\cdot\!\cdot y_{n})\;{\left|\left.\!\!\>y\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}\;,

(80e)

\displaystyle{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZH-gray-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\,g_{m{+}n}\!\mathop{\;\sum\sum\;}_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{m}\!\!\>,}\,{y\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{n}}\\[1.50694pt]
\sum\limits_{h}x_{h}+\sum\limits_{k}y_{k}\;\!=\,0\end{subarray}}}\,\left|y\right\rangle\!\!\left\langle x\right|

\displaystyle=\;g_{m{+}n}\!\mathop{\;\sum\sum\;}_{\mathclap{{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{m}\!\!\>,}\,{y\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{n}}}}\left\langle\big.\,\smash{\textstyle\sum\limits_{h}x_{h}+\sum\limits_{k}y_{k}}\,\!\!\>\left|\>\!0\>\!\right\rangle\right.\,\left|y\right\rangle\!\!\left\langle x\right|

\displaystyle=\,g_{m{+}n}\cdot\nu^{m{+}n{+}2}\mathop{\;\sum\sum\;}_{\mathclap{{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{m}\!\!\>,}\,{y\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{n}}}}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;\big.\,\smash{\textstyle\sum\limits_{h}x_{h}+\sum\limits_{k}y_{k}}\,\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!\>\!0\>\!\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\,\,{\left|\left.\!\!\>y\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}

\displaystyle=\,g_{m{+}n}\cdot\nu^{-m{-}n{+}2}\mathop{\int\!\!\!\!\int}\limits_{\mathclap{{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{m}\!\!\>,}\,{y\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}^{n}}}}\,{\left|\left.\!\!\>y\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}\;\;{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;\big.\,\smash{\textstyle\sum\limits_{h}x_{h}+\sum\limits_{k}y_{k}}\,\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!0\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;.

(80g)

In particular, the imposed semantics for the generalised-not dot are automatically satisfied by the definition of the point-mass vectors
{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}
; requiring the leading scalar on the last line of Eqn. (
80
) to be equal to
1
, imposes the constraint
u_{k}=\nu^{-k{+}2}
(which in particular is consistent with
u_{2}=1
); requiring the leasing scalar on the last line of Eqn. (
80
) to be
1
, imposes the constraint
h_{k}=\nu^{k}
(which in particular is consistent with
h_{0}=1
); and requiring the leading scalar of Eqn. (
80
) to be equal to
1
, imposes the constraint
g_{k}=\nu^{k-2}
.

Note that none of the above imposes constraints on
\nu
itself, essentially because the only unitarity constraints happen to involve a single integral over
{\mathbf{D}}
(as with the generalised-not dot or the
1\to 1
white dot), so that all factors of
\nu
cancel in those cases.
Thus, the approach of defining semantics for ZH generators in terms of integrals as in Eqn. (
29
) is in itself sufficient to ensure the Ockhamicity of the interpretation, regardless of the normalising factor
\nu
is used to define the measure
\mu
.

We note in particular that in the case
D=2
, the original semantics for ZH diagrams presented by Backens and Kissinger
[
30
]
satisfies these constraints for
\nu=1
.
For arbitrary
D>1
, such a choice yields a measure for which
\mu(\{\ast\})=1
and
\mu({\mathbf{D}})=D
.
While the rewrite systems that one obtains for this measure are likely to involve more frequent changes to the scalar factors through scalar gadgets, this does seem (both intuitively and in practise
[
35
,
40
]
) an appropriate choice to denote and analyse problems in counting complexity.

B.3
Ockhamic semantics for ZX diagrams

By considering Ockhamic semantics for ZX generators, we necessarily consider an interpretation of the (inverse) discrete Fourier transform which is unitary.

If we impose the constraint that the inverse Fourier transform as expressed in Eqn. (
25
) should be equal to the quantum Fourier transform, this is equivalent to imposing unitarity on a Fourier transform as expressed in Eqn. (
24
) that preserves the measure.
From this, we would obtain the constraint
\nu=D^{-1/4}
, as described in Section
3.2
.
We can also see this by directly considering the consequences of imposing this constraint on the meaning of integration over
{\mathbf{D}}
:

\displaystyle\text{\small$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{D}}$}\mathop{\sum\sum}_{x,k\in{\mathbf{D}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi ikx/D}\left|k\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|\,=\,{\Bigl[\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigl[\,\smash{\raisebox{-2.5pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZX-H-plus-box.pdf}\end{gathered}$}}\,\Bigr]\mspace{-5.5mu}\Bigr]}\,:={}

\displaystyle\mathop{\int\!\!\!\!\int}\limits_{\;\mathclap{k,x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi ikx/D}\;{\left|\left.\!\!\>k\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}

(81)

\displaystyle{}={}

\displaystyle\nu^{2}\mathop{\sum\sum}\limits_{\;\mathclap{k,x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi ikx/D}\;\left|k\right\rangle\left\langle x\right|\;,

so that
\nu=D^{-1/4}
, and in particular
\mu({\mathbf{D}})=N=D\nu^{2}=\sqrt{D}
.
In this way, unlike the case with Ockhamic semantic map of ZH generators as we considered in Section
B.2
, relating Ockhamic semantics of ZX generators to simple integrals necessarily constrains
\mu
.

Following Section
B.2
, to obtain a simple representation of the semantics for green and red dots in an Ockhamic semantic map, we might impose the following constraints:

\displaystyle{}\mspace{-24mu}{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.31248pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZX-green-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}^{\!\otimes n}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle x\right.\!\right\rvert}^{\!\!\;\otimes m}\,,

\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt{\Biggl[\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggl[\,\smash{\!\!\!\raisebox{-2.31248pt}{$\begin{gathered}\includegraphics[]{./figures/ZX-red-dot-arity.pdf}\end{gathered}$}\!\!}\,\Biggr]\mspace{-7.5mu}\Biggr]}

\displaystyle=\int\limits_{\mathclap{k\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\left|\left.\!\!\>\smash{\omega^{-k}}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}^{\!\otimes n}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\smash{\!\;\omega^{k}\!\;}\right.\!\right\rvert}^{\!\!\;\otimes m}\!\;.\mspace{-18mu}

As with the white dots in Ockhamic semantic maps of the ZH calculus (which is identical to the analysis of green dots with phase function
\tilde{\theta}(x)=1
), we would then obtain the constraint
u_{k}=\nu^{-k{+}2}
.

B.4
Relationship to the ‘well-tempered’ calculi for
D=2

Notice that the normalisation
\nu=D^{-1/4}
, and the corresponding semantics, essentially reproduces
19
19

19

Strictly speaking, the calculi of Ref.
[
19
]
involve red and green dots with parameters
\theta\in{\mathbb{R}}
, H-boxes with parameters
\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}
, only one type of Hadamard box instead of two, and a ‘nu box’ which is missing from the calculus presented here.
We may bridge these differences using the short-hand described for phases / amplitudes to parameterise these nodes, identifying the Hadamard plus and minus boxes with the single Hadamard box of Ref.
[
19
]
, and replacing the nu-boxes with some suitable scalar gadgets (such as H-boxes parameterised by powers of
\nu=D^{-1/4}
).

the ‘well-tempered’ semantics of ZX and ZH diagrams
[
19
]
in the case that
D=2
.
In this way, Eqns. (
28
) and (
29
) provide a more intuitive definition of those semantics, and extend them to arbitrary
D>1
.

The process by which we obtain the semantic map in Section
3.2

may appear very different from how the well-tempered interpretation was devised in Ref.
[
19
]
, which solved for a specific Ockhamic semantic map subject to a list of desirable (idealised) rewrites.
However: it is worth noting that the framework of discrete integrals and (what we have here called) ‘accompanying’ point-mass distributions, implicitly impose some of the constraints that were explicitly imposed in Ref.
[
19
]
.
Specifically: by choosing our notation so that

\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}^{\otimes n}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;x\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!a\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;\;=\;\;{\left|\left.\!\!\>a\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}^{\otimes n},

(84)

it is not difficult to show that we automatically ensure the correctness of a number of rewrites including
(ZX-GF)
,
(ZX-CPY)
,
(ZX-PU)
,
(ZH-AI)
,
(ZH-NS)
,
(ZH-WGB)
, and
(ZH-HM)
for the semantics of Eqns. (
28
) and (
29
).
In this way, we may regard the framework of discrete integrals and accompanying point-mass distributions as simplifying both the results and the methodology of Ref.
[
19
]
.
This provides a clarification and a theoretical justification of the ‘well-tempered’ semantics, and indeed an extension of them to all
D>1
.

Note that choosing the interpretations of Eqn. (
29
) just for the ZH generators, does not in fact impose any constraints on either the measure
\mu
on
{\mathbf{D}}
.
As we see in Section
B.2
, Eqn. (
29
) only imposes the constraint on the interpretation that the generators must be related to each other by simple geometric progressions related to the parameter
\nu
, but does not fix what
\nu
should be.
In particular, if we take
{\nu\!=\!1}
, Eqn. (
29
) reproduces the original semantics provided by Backens and Kissinger
[
30
]
for the ZH generators for
{D\!=\!2}
.
In effect, the ZH calculus prioritises the standard basis to such an extent that it does not impose any strong relationships between that basis and any other, and in so doing leaves
\nu
unconstrained.
It is the single constraint on the ZX generators, that
{\left|\left.\!\!\>\smash{\omega^{k}}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}=\int_{x}\omega^{-kx}\,{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}
should be unitarily equivalent to
{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}
, which suffices to fix the measure
\mu
and thus to fix specific semantics for all of the generators through Eqns. (
28
) and (
29
).

B.5
Considering alternative normalisations of the Fourier transform

Given the decisive role that fixing the interpretation of the discrete Fourier transform plays in constraining semantic maps for ZX and ZH diagrams, it may be of interest to consider how choosing a different normalisation factor
\nu
would affect the presentation of the Fourier transform, or the relationships between the measures of the domain of a function
f:({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu)\to{\mathbb{C}}
and that of
\hat{f}
.

Above, we described the way in which the measure
\mu
on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
(induced from the measure on
{\mathbf{D}}
defined in Section
3
) is constrained by various constraints on the discrete Fourier transform, construed as a map
f\mapsto\hat{f}
on functions
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
.
In particular, if we consider
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
as a measure space and take
f:({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu)\to{\mathbb{C}}
and
\hat{f}:({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu)\to{\mathbb{C}}
to have the same domain considered as measure spaces, and if we also take
F:{\left|\left.\!\!\>f\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\mapsto{\left|\left.\!\!\>\smash{\hat{f}}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}
as defined in Eqn. (
24
) to be unitary, we find that
N=\mu({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})=\sqrt{D}
(or equivalently,
\nu=\smash{{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;x\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!x\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}}^{-1/2}=D^{-1/4}
).

If one wished instead to have a more general relation
N=\lambda D
for some scalar
\lambda\neq D^{-1/2}
, one could instead consider

•

setting
F^{\dagger}F=\alpha\mathbf{1}
for a scalar
\alpha>0
, which is equal to
1
if and only if
F
is unitary;

•

Defining
\hat{f}
to range over the space
({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu^{\prime})
for a measure
\mu^{\prime}=\beta\mu
for some scalar
\beta>0
;

•

Defining the Fourier transform
\hat{f}
of
f
by modifying Eqn. (
20
) to incorporate an additional scalar factor
\gamma>0
which may differ from
1
.

We consider the consequences of all three such modifications.
Let
\mathbf{X}_{\{0\}}:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
be the function such that
\mathbf{X}_{\{0\}}(t)=1
if and only if
t=0
, and
\mathbf{X}_{\{0\}}(t)=0
otherwise; then

{\left|\left.\!\!\>\smash{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in({\mathbb{Z}}_{\!\!\;D}\!\!\;,\!\;\mu)}}\mathbf{X}_{\{0\}}(x)\;{\left|\left.\!\!\>x\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;=\;\nu^{2}{\left|\left.\!\!\>0\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;=\;\nu\left|0\right\rangle,

(85)

from which it follows that

\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}(k)\;=\;\gamma\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in({\mathbb{Z}}_{\!\!\;D}\!\!\;,\!\;\mu)}}\mathbf{X}_{\{0\}}(x)\;{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi ikx/D}\;=\;\gamma\nu^{2}.

(86)

Let
\mathrm{J}:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
be the constant function
\mathrm{J}(x)=1
: then
\mathrm{J}=\tfrac{1}{\gamma\nu^{2}}\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}
.
For the sake of uniformity, define point-mass functions
{\left|\left.\!\!\>k\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}
to accompany the integrals over
k\in({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu^{\prime})
for
\mu^{\prime}=\beta\mu
, so that

\int\limits_{\mathclap{k\in({\mathbb{Z}}_{\!\!\;D}\!\!\;,\!\;\mu^{\prime})}}{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;k\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!k\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;\mathrm{d}\mu^{\prime}(k)\;=\;1.

(87)

Using the fact that
\nu^{2}=\mu(\{\ast\})=N/D
, we then have

\displaystyle N\;=\;\mu({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in({\mathbb{Z}}_{\!\!\;D}\!\!\;,\!\;\mu)}}1\;\mathrm{d}\mu(x)

\displaystyle=\;\beta\!\int\limits_{\mathclap{k\in({\mathbb{Z}}_{\!\!\;D}\!\!\;,\!\;\mu^{\prime})}}1\;\mathrm{d}\mu^{\prime}(k)

(88)

\displaystyle=\;\beta\!\mathop{\int\!\!\!\!\int}\limits_{\mathclap{h,k\in({\mathbb{Z}}_{\!\!\;D}\!\!\;,\!\;\mu^{\prime})}}\mathrm{J}(h)^{\ast}\mathrm{J}(k)\;{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;h\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!k\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;\mathrm{d}\mu^{\prime}(h)\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{\prime}(k)

\displaystyle=\;\beta\,{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;\mathrm{J}\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!\mathrm{J}\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;=\;\frac{\beta}{\gamma^{2}\nu^{4}}\,{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;\smash{\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}}\big.\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!\big.\smash{\widehat{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}}\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}

\displaystyle=\;\frac{\beta}{\gamma^{2}\nu^{4}}\,{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\smash{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}\big.\right.\!\right\rvert}F^{\dagger}F{\left|\left.\!\!\>\big.\smash{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}

\displaystyle=\;\frac{\alpha\beta}{\gamma^{2}\nu^{4}}\,{\left\langle\mspace{-4.25mu}\left\langle\left.\!\!\;\smash{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}\big.\>\!\right|\mspace{-8mu}\left|\>\!\big.\smash{\mathbf{X}}_{\{0\}}\right.\!\!\>\right\rangle\mspace{-4.25mu}\right\rangle}\;=\;\frac{\alpha\beta}{\gamma^{2}\nu^{2}}\;=\;\frac{\alpha\beta D}{\gamma^{2}N},

so that
N\;=\;{\sqrt{\alpha\beta D}}/{\gamma}\,.
Thus, we may vary any three of
\alpha
,
\beta
,
\gamma
, and
N
to determine the remaining parameter.

If one wished to fix a different value for
N
(
e.g.
,
N\!\!\>=\!\!\>1
or
N\!\!\>=\!\!\>D
), and separately fix the extent to which
F
increases or decreases the
\ell_{2}
norm of its operands (if one wished to adopt a convention where
F
might not be a unitary matrix), this would determine the extent to which the difference in the norm of
\smash{\hat{f}}
corresponds to a change of units
\mu
to
\mu^{\prime}
as we transform
f\mapsto\hat{f}
, or to which Eqn. (
20
) must be rescaled, or both.
Instead, we elect to fix
\alpha,\beta,\gamma=1
, which allows us to take Eqn. (
20
) unmodified, to consider only one measure
\mu
on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
in the context of the Fourier transform, and to take
F
to be unitary.
This imposes the constraint
N=\sqrt{D}
, or equivalently
\nu=D^{-1/4}
.

While these remarks stand apart from any analysis over
{\mathbb{R}}
, it is possible to show how relating the measure
\mu
on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
to a discrete measure on the compact continuous group
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
further motivates distinct measures
\mu,\mu^{\prime}
for the domains of
f:({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu)\to{\mathbb{C}}
and that of
\hat{f}:({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu^{\prime})\to{\mathbb{C}}
, if one fixes
N
to be different from
\sqrt{D}
.
See Appendix
D.3.4
for more details.

Appendix C
Quadratic Gaussian integrals

In this Section, we consider how to evaluate the quadratic Gauss integrals described in Eqn. (
40
).

C.1
Preliminaries on quadratic Gaussian sums

The scalars in Eqn. (
40
) may be expressed in terms of quadratic Gaussian sums, which are sums of the form

G(r,s,N)\;=\;\sum_{x=0}^{N{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/N}\;=\;\sum_{x=0}^{N{-}1}\omega_{N}^{rx^{2}+sx}

(89)

where
\omega_{N}=\exp(2\pi i/N)
is a primitive
N\textsuperscript{th}
root of unity.
Motivated by the analysis of Ref.
[
49
]
, we consider two separate cases: the case where
N
is odd, and the case where
N
is a multiple of
4
.
(The case where
N
is even but not a multiple of
4
does not arise in our work, as we consider
N=D
for
D
odd, and
N=2D
for
D
even, where
D>1
is the dimension of a qudit.)

We define the Jacobi symbol
\bigl(\frac{k}{m}\bigr)
for
m
and odd integer and
k\in{\mathbb{Z}}
, as follows.
Let
\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}_{p}
be the quadratic character on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{p}
:

\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}_{p}(k)\;=\;\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $p$ divides $k$};\\
+1,&\text{if $k\equiv u^{2}\pmod{p}$ for some $u\in[p]$};\\
-1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(90)

For
m=p_{1}^{t_{1}}p_{2}^{t_{2}}\cdots p_{n}^{t_{n}}
an odd integer with
p_{j}
distinct primes and
t_{1}\in{\mathbb{N}}
, we define the Jacobi symbol as

\Bigl(\frac{h}{m}\Bigr)\;=\;\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}_{p_{1}}(k)^{t_{1}}\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}_{p_{2}}(k)^{t_{2}}\,\cdots\,\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}_{p_{n}}(k)^{t_{n}}\,,

(91)

which is
0
is
k
and
m
have any common prime factors
p_{j}
, and is
\pm 1
otherwise.
For odd integers
r
, we also define

\varepsilon_{m}\;=\;\left\{\begin{aligned} 1,\;\;&\quad\text{if $m\equiv 1\pmod{4}$}\\
i,\;\;&\quad\text{if $m\equiv 3\pmod{4}$}\end{aligned}\right\}\;=\;i^{(m-1)^{2}/4},

(92)

which satisfies
\varepsilon_{m}^{2}=\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}{\raisebox{0.80728pt}{$\chi$}}_{m}(-1)
.
Suppose that
r
and
N
have a common divisor other than
1
.
Let
t=\gcd(r,N)
.
It is possible to show that

G(r,s,N)\;=\;\begin{cases}t\cdot G\Bigl(\dfrac{r}{t},\dfrac{s}{t},\dfrac{N}{t}\Bigr),&\text{if $t$ is a divisor of $s$};\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(93)

We can then reduce the general case, to the special case where
r
and
N
have no common divisor
t>1
, and where
r\geqslant 0
.
Suppose, then, that
r
and
N
have no common divisor
t>1
, so that
r
has an inverse
u\in[N]
modulo
N
(
i.e.
,
ur\equiv 1\bmod{N}
), and
N
has an inverse
q\in[r]
modulo
r
(
i.e.
,
qN\equiv q\bmod{r}
).

•

If
N
is odd, let
h\in{\mathbf{D}}
be such that
2h\equiv 1\pmod{N}
, and let
\tilde{s}=uhs
so that
2r\tilde{s}\equiv s\pmod{N}
.
We then have

\displaystyle G(r,s,N)\;=\;\sum_{x=0}^{N{-}1}\omega_{N}^{r(x-\tilde{s})^{2}+s(x-\tilde{s})}

\displaystyle=\;\sum_{x=0}^{N{-}1}\omega_{N}^{r(x^{2}-2\tilde{s}x+\tilde{s}^{2})+sx-s\tilde{s}}

(94)

\displaystyle=\;\sum_{x=0}^{N{-}1}\omega_{N}^{rx^{2}+\;\!ru^{2}h^{2}s^{2}\;\!-\;\!uhs^{2}}

\displaystyle=\;\omega_{N}^{ru^{2}(h-h^{2})s^{2}}\!\cdot G(r,0,N).

For
N
odd and
r
having no factors in common with
N
greater than
1
,

G(r,0,N)\;=\;\varepsilon_{N}\Bigl(\frac{r}{N}\Bigr)\sqrt{N}

(95)

where
\bigl(\tfrac{r}{N}\bigr)
is the Jacobi symbol.
Then we have

G(r,s,N)\;\;=\;\;\omega_{N}^{ru^{2}(h-h^{2})s^{2}}\!\varepsilon_{N}\Bigl(\frac{r}{N}\Bigr)\sqrt{N}\;\;=\;\;{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi iru^{2}(h-h^{2})s^{2}\!\!\;/N}\,i^{(N-1)^{2}\!\!\>/\!\!\;4}\,\Bigl(\frac{r}{N}\Bigr)\sqrt{N}

(96)

In particular, we have
\bigl\lvert G(r,s,N)\bigr\rvert=\sqrt{N}
, and for
s=0
we have
G(r,s,N)=i^{k}\sqrt{N}
for some
k\in{\mathbb{Z}}
.

•

Suppose that
N
is even (in which case
r
must be odd as it would not be divisible by
2
)
Let
N=2M
for some integer
M
.
We may consider the alternative sum

\tilde{G}(r,s,M)\;=\;\sum_{x=0}^{M{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/M},

(97)

which we may relate to
G(r,s,N)
as follows:

{}\mspace{-18mu}\begin{aligned} G(r,s,2M)\;&=\sum_{x=0}^{M{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/2M}+\sum_{x=M}^{2M{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/2M}\\
&=\sum_{x=0}^{M{-}1}\Bigl[{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/M}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i\bigl(r(M^{2}+2Mx+x^{2})+s(M+x)\bigr)/M}\Bigr]\\
&=\sum_{x=0}^{M{-}1}\Bigl[{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/M}\,+\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(Mr+s)}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/M}\Bigr]\\
&=\Bigl(1+(-1)^{Mr+s}\Bigr)\;\!\tilde{G}(r,s,M)\;.\end{aligned}

(98)

If
M
is odd and
s
is even, then we have
(-1)^{Mr+s}=-1
, in which case
G(r,s,N)=0
; similarly if
M
is even and
s
is odd.
Thus it suffices to consider the cases where
M
and
s
are either both even, or both odd, so that
Mr+s
is even.

[(a)]

1.

If
M,s
are both odd, let
g\in{\mathbb{Z}}
be such that
2g=u(M-s)
, where recall
u\equiv r^{-1}\pmod{2M}
.

\displaystyle{}\mspace{-18mu}G(r,s,2M)\;

\displaystyle=\sum_{x=0}^{2M{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/2M}

\displaystyle=\sum_{x=0}^{2M{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i(r(x+g)^{2}+s(x+g)/2M}

\displaystyle=\sum_{x=0}^{2M{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i(rx^{2}+2grx+rg^{2}+sx+sg)/2M}

\displaystyle=\;{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rg^{2}+sg)/M}\sum_{x=0}^{2M{-}1}(-1)^{x}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi irx^{2}/M}

\displaystyle={\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rg^{2}+sg)/M}\sum_{x=0}^{M{-}1}\Bigl((-1)^{x}{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi irx^{2}/M}\,+\,(-1)^{x}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi ir(M+x)^{2}/M}\Bigr)

\displaystyle={\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rg^{2}+sg)/M}\sum_{x=0}^{M{-}1}\Bigl((-1)^{x}{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi irx^{2}/M}\,-\,(-1)^{x}{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi irx^{2}/M}\Bigr)\;=\;0\;.

(99)

Together with the fact that
G(r,s,N)=0
for
M
odd and
s
even, we have in fact
G(r,s,N)=0
if
N=2M
for
M\in{\mathbb{Z}}
odd.

2.

If
M,s
are both even, let
M^{\prime},s^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{Z}}
be such that
M=2M^{\prime}
and
s=2s^{\prime}
.
Let
\varsigma=+1
if
r>0
and
\varsigma=-1
if
r<0
.
We may show that

\displaystyle\tilde{G}(r,s,M)

\displaystyle=\sum_{x=0}^{M{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(rx^{2}+sx)/M}

(100)

\displaystyle=\,\sqrt{\lvert Mr^{-1}\rvert\;\!}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i\bigl(\lvert Mr\rvert-s^{2}\bigr)\!\!\;\big/\!\!\>4Mr}\sum_{k=0}^{\lvert r\rvert{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{-\pi i(Mk^{2}+sk)/r}

\displaystyle=\,\sqrt{\lvert Mr^{-1}\rvert}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\varsigma i\pi/4}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-i\pi s^{2}\!\!\>/4Mr}\sum_{k=0}^{\lvert r\rvert{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{-\varsigma\;\!i\pi(Mk^{2}+sk)\big/\lvert r\rvert}

\displaystyle=\;\sqrt{\lvert Mr^{-1}\rvert}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\varsigma i\pi/4}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-i\pi s^{2}\!\!\>/4Mr}\,\tilde{G}(-\varsigma M,\,-\varsigma s,\,\lvert r\rvert),

by quadratic reciprocity.
By Eqn. (
98
), we have

\displaystyle G\bigl(-\varsigma M,-\varsigma s,\lvert r\rvert\bigr)

\displaystyle=\;\Bigl(1+(-1)^{Mr+s}\Bigr)\,\tilde{G}\bigl(-\varsigma M,-\varsigma s,\lvert r\rvert\bigr)

(101)

\displaystyle=\;2\,\tilde{G}\bigl(-\varsigma M,-\varsigma s,\lvert r\rvert\bigr)\;=\;2\,\tilde{G}\bigl(\varsigma M,\varsigma s,\lvert r\rvert\bigr)^{\ast}\;.

Recall that
r
is odd, and has no common divisors
t>1
with
N
; it then follows that
r
has no such common divisors with
M
either, and in particular, we have
(4q)M^{\prime}=qN\equiv 1\pmod{r}
.
Let
\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}
be such that
\eta\equiv 2^{-1}\pmod{r}
: we then have

\mspace{-36mu}\begin{aligned} G(r,s,N)\;&=\;2\,\tilde{G}(r,s,M)\\[4.30554pt]
&=\;2\,\sqrt{\lvert Mr^{-1}\rvert}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{\varsigma i\pi/4}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-i\pi s^{2}\!\!\>/4Mr}\,\tilde{G}\bigl(\varsigma M,\varsigma s,\lvert r\rvert\bigr)^{\ast}\\[8.61108pt]
&=\;\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert Nr^{-1}\rvert}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{\varsigma i\pi/4}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-\pi is^{2}\!\!\>/2Nr}\,G\bigl(\varsigma 2M^{\prime},\varsigma 2s^{\prime},2\lvert r\rvert\bigr)^{\ast}\\[8.61108pt]
&=\;\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert Nr^{-1}\rvert}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{\varsigma i\pi/4}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-\pi is^{2}\!\!\>/2Nr}\,\cdot 2\cdot G\bigl(\varsigma M^{\prime},\varsigma s^{\prime},\lvert r\rvert\bigr)^{\ast}\\[8.61108pt]
&=\;\sqrt{2\lvert Nr^{-1}\rvert}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{\varsigma i\pi/4}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-\varsigma\pi is^{2}\!\!\>\big/2N\lvert r\rvert}\,\biggl({\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i\varsigma M^{\prime}(4q)^{2}(\eta^{2}-\eta)s^{2}\!\!\;/\lvert r\rvert}\;i^{-(\lvert r\rvert-1)^{2}\!\!\>/\!\!\;4}\,\Bigl(\frac{M^{\prime}}{\lvert r\rvert}\Bigr)\sqrt{\lvert r\rvert}\biggr)\mspace{-90mu}\\[4.30554pt]
&=\;{\mathrm{e}}^{\varsigma i\pi/4}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{-\varsigma\pi is^{2}\!\!\>\big/2N\lvert r\rvert}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi i\varsigma qs^{2}\!\!\;/\lvert r\rvert}\;i^{-(\lvert r\rvert-1)^{2}\!\!\>/\!\!\;4}\,\Bigl(\frac{N}{\lvert r\rvert}\Bigr)\cdot\sqrt{2N\;\!}\\[4.30554pt]
&=\;{\mathrm{e}}^{i\pi\varsigma/4}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{-\pi i\varsigma s^{2}(1+4Nq)\!\!\>\big/\!\!\>N\lvert r\rvert}\;i^{-(\lvert r\rvert-1)^{2}\!\!\>/\!\!\;4}\,\Bigl(\frac{N}{\lvert r\rvert}\Bigr)\cdot\sqrt{2N\;\!}\,.\end{aligned}

(102)

In particular, we have
\bigl\lvert G(r,s,N)\bigr\rvert=\sqrt{2N}
, and for
s=0
we have
G(r,s,N)=\sqrt{i}^{\,k}\!\cdot\sqrt{2N}
for some odd integer
k\in{\mathbb{Z}}
.

In summary, if
r
and
N
have no common divisor
t>1
, we have:

\displaystyle\mspace{-12mu}G(r,s,N)\,

\displaystyle=\,\left\{\begin{aligned} {\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi(r,s,N)}\sqrt{N},\quad&\text{if $N$ is odd};\\
{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi(r,s,N)}\sqrt{2N},\quad&\text{if $N$ is a multiple of $4$ and $s$ is even},\\
0,\quad&\text{otherwise},\end{aligned}\right.

(103a)

where
\varphi(r,s,N)\in{\mathbb{R}}
is some phase angle satisfying

\displaystyle\mspace{-18mu}{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi(r,s,N)}\,

\displaystyle=\,\left\{\begin{aligned} {\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi iru^{2}(h-h^{2})s^{2}\!\!\;/N}\,i^{(N-1)^{2}\!\!\>/\!\!\;4}\,\Bigl(\frac{r}{N}\Bigr),&\quad\begin{minipage}[107.63855pt]if $N$ is odd \\
\small(for
$u\equiv r^{-1}\!\bmod{N}$ \\
and
$h\equiv 2^{-1}\!\bmod{N}$),
\end{minipage}\\[4.30554pt]
{\mathrm{e}}^{i\pi\varsigma/4}\;{\mathrm{e}}^{-\pi i\varsigma s^{2}(1+4Nq)\!\!\>\big/\!\!\>N\lvert r\rvert}\;i^{-(\lvert r\rvert-1)^{2}\!\!\>/\!\!\;4}\,\Bigl(\frac{N}{\lvert r\rvert}\Bigr),&\quad\begin{minipage}[107.63855pt]if $N$ is even \\
\small(for $q\equiv N^{-1}\!\bmod{r}$),
\end{minipage}\end{aligned}\right.\mspace{-24mu}

(103b)

where
\bigl(\tfrac{r}{N}\bigr)
and
\bigl(\tfrac{N}{r}\bigr)
are Jacobi symbols as described by Eqn. (
91
).
In particular, note that if
s=0
then
{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi(r,s,N)}
is a power of
{\mathrm{e}}^{i\pi/4}
, and in particular is equal to
{\mathrm{e}}^{i\pi(N+1)k/4}
for some integer
k
.
Using Eqn. (
93
) to generalise this to include the case where
t=\gcd(r,N)
may be greater than
1
, we then have

\displaystyle G(r,s,N)

\displaystyle=\,\left\{\begin{aligned} {\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{r}{t},\,\tfrac{s}{t},\,\tfrac{N}{t}\bigr)}\cdot\sqrt{tN},\quad&\text{if $N/t$ is odd, and $s$ is a multiple of $t$};\\
{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{r}{t},\,\tfrac{s}{t},\,\tfrac{N}{t}\bigr)}\cdot\sqrt{2tN},\quad&\mathrlap{\text{if $N/t$ is a multiple of $4$, and $s$ is a multiple of $2t$};}\\[4.30554pt]
0,\quad&\text{otherwise},\end{aligned}\right.

(104)

using the fact that when
G(r,s,N)
is non-zero, we have
\bigl\lvert G(r,s,N)\bigr\rvert=t\cdot\bigl\lvert G(\tfrac{r}{t},\tfrac{s}{t},\tfrac{N}{t})\bigr\rvert
, which is equal to
t\cdot\sqrt{N/t\,}=\sqrt{tN}
for
N
odd and equal to
t\cdot\sqrt{2N/t\,}=\sqrt{2tN}
for
N
even.

C.2
Application to quadratic Gaussian integrals

In our analysis, we consider two sorts of integrals, depending on the parity of the qudit dimension
D
.
In each case, we are interested in the integral

\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}\tau^{2ax+bx^{2}}\;=\;\nu^{2}\,\sum\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}\,\tau^{2ax+bx^{2}}\;,

(105)

where
\tau={\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(D^{2}+1)/D}
and
\nu=D^{-1/4}
.
For all integers
D>1
, we have
\tau^{2}={\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(2D^{2}+2)/D}={\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i+2\pi i/D}={\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i/D}
.
However, for
D
odd,
\tau
is itself also a
D\textsuperscript{th}
root of unity (specifically:
\tau=\omega^{h}
for
h\equiv 2^{-1}\bmod{D}
), whereas for
D
even we have
\tau={\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i/D}
, which is a primitive
2D\textsuperscript{th}
root of unity.

For
D
an odd integer.

In the case of
D
odd, we are interested in the quantity

\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}\tau^{2ax+bx^{2}}\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi ih(2ax+bx^{2})/D}.

(106)

Using the definition of the integral and the normalisation
\nu=D^{-1/4}
, we have

\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\nu^{2}\sum_{x=0}^{D{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi i(2ahx+bhx^{2})/D}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{D}}G(bh,a,D).

(107)

If
t=\gcd(b,D)
, we may apply Eqn. (
104
) to obtain

\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\left\{\begin{aligned} \frac{\text{\small$\sqrt{Dt}$}}{\text{\small$\sqrt{D}$}}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{bh}{t},\tfrac{a}{t},\tfrac{D}{t}\bigr)}\;&=\;\sqrt{t\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{bh}{t},\tfrac{a}{t},\tfrac{D}{t}\bigr)}\;,&&\text{if $a$ is also a multiple of $t$};\\[4.30554pt]
&\phantom{=}\;\;\;0,&&\text{otherwise};\end{aligned}\right.

(108)

in particular, if
t=1
, we have
\lvert\Gamma(a,b,D)\rvert=1
.

For
D
an even integer.

In the case of
D
even, we are interested in the quantity

\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}\tau^{2ax+bx^{2}}\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbf{D}}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(2ax+bx^{2})/D}.

(109)

Again using the definition of the integral and the normalisation
\nu=D^{-1/4}
, we have

\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\nu^{2}\sum_{x=0}^{D{-}1}{\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(2ax+bx^{2})/D}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\tilde{G}(b,2a,D)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{D}}G(b,2a,2D),

(110)

where
\tilde{G}(b,2a,D)
is as defined in Eqn. (
97
).
Note that as
D
is even,
2D
is then a multiple of
4
.
Let
v=\gcd(b,2D)
: we may again apply Eqn. (
104
) to obtain

\displaystyle{}\mspace{-36mu}\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\left\{\begin{aligned} \frac{\text{\small$\sqrt{4Dv}$}}{\text{\small$2\sqrt{D}$}}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{v},\tfrac{2a}{v},\tfrac{2D}{v}\bigr)}\;&=\;\sqrt{v\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{v},\tfrac{2a}{v},\tfrac{2D}{v}\bigr)}\;,&&\mathrlap{\begin{minipage}[129.16626pt]if $2D/v$ is a multiple of $4$ \\
and $2a$ is a multiple of $2v$;
\end{minipage}}\\[8.61108pt]
\frac{\text{\small$\sqrt{2Dv}$}}{\text{\small$2\sqrt{D}$}}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{v},\tfrac{2a}{v},\tfrac{2D}{v}\bigr)}\;&=\;\sqrt{v\!\!\>/2\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{v},\tfrac{2a}{v},\tfrac{2D}{v}\bigr)}\;,&&\mathrlap{\begin{minipage}[129.16626pt]if $2D/v$ is odd and \\
$2a$ is a multiple of $v$;
\end{minipage}}\\[8.61108pt]
0\;,&&&\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.\mspace{-36mu}

Again, let
t=\gcd(b,D)
.
Furthermore, let
g,g^{\prime}
be the largest integers such that
2^{g}
divides
D
,and
2^{g^{\prime}}
divides
b
.
For
q=\min\;\{g,g^{\prime}\}
, this means that
2^{q}
is the largest power of
2
which divides
t
.
Let
t^{\prime}=t/2^{q}
, and
D^{\prime}=D/2^{g}t^{\prime}
and
b^{\prime}=b\!\>/\!\>2^{g^{\prime}}\!t^{\prime}
: then all of
t^{\prime}
,
D^{\prime}
, and
b^{\prime}
are odd integers with no common divisors greater than
1
, and
D=2^{g}t^{\prime}D^{\prime}=2^{g-q}tD^{\prime}
and
b=2^{g^{\prime}}t^{\prime}b^{\prime}=2^{g^{\prime}-q}tb^{\prime}
.
Then

v\;=\;\gcd(b,2D)\;=\;\gcd\bigl(2^{g^{\prime}}t^{\prime}b^{\prime},2^{g+1}t^{\prime}D^{\prime}\bigr)\;=\;2^{\,\min\,\{g+1,g^{\prime}\}}\cdot t^{\prime}

(112)

We may then present the cases in Eqn. (
) as follows.

•

If
2D/v=2^{g+1-\min\{g+1,g^{\prime}\}}D^{\prime}
is a multiple of
4
, then
g+1-\min\{g{+}1,g^{\prime}\}>1
, from which we may infer that
g{+}1-g^{\prime}>1
and that
g-g^{\prime}>0
.
Then
q=g^{\prime}
and
v=t
; and we have
D/t
even and
b/t
odd.
Conversely, if
D/t
is even, this also implies that
g-g^{\prime}>0
, and that
2D/v
is a multiple of
4
.
(Notice also that in this case,
2a
is a multiple of
2v
if and only if
a
is a multiple of
t
).

•

If
2D/v=2^{g+1-\min\{g+1,g^{\prime}\}}D^{\prime}
is odd, then
g{+}1\leqslant g^{\prime}
.
In this case we would have
q=g<g^{\prime}
and
v=2^{q+1}t^{\prime}=2t
; and we have
D/t
odd and
b/t
even.
Conversely, if
D/t
is odd and
b/t
is even, this implies that
q=g<g^{\prime}
, which in turn implies that
2D/v
is odd.
(In this case as well,
2a
is a multiple of
v
if and only if
a
is a multiple of
t
.)

From these observations, in the case of
D
even, we obtain

\displaystyle\Gamma(a,b,D)\;=\;\left\{\begin{aligned} \sqrt{t\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{t},\tfrac{2a}{t},\tfrac{2D}{t}\bigr)}\;,&\qquad\begin{minipage}[236.80481pt]if $D$ is even, $D/t$ is even, $b/t$ is odd, \\
and
$a$ is a multiple of $t$;
\end{minipage}\\[2.15277pt]
\sqrt{t\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{2t},\tfrac{a}{t},\tfrac{D}{t}\bigr)}\;,&\qquad\begin{minipage}[236.80481pt]if $D$ is even, $D/t$ is odd, $b/t$ is even, \\
and
$a$ is a multiple of $t$;
\end{minipage}\\[4.30554pt]
0\;,&\qquad\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.\mspace{-72mu}

Summary.

From the equations above, if
t=\gcd(b,D)
, we have

\displaystyle{}\mspace{-36mu}\Gamma(a,b,D)\,=\,\left\{\begin{aligned} \sqrt{t\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{t},\tfrac{2a}{t},\tfrac{2D}{t}\bigr)},&\quad\!\!\text{if $D$ and $D/t$ are even but $b/t$ is odd, and $a$ is a multiple of $t$;
}\\[4.30554pt]
\sqrt{t\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{b}{2t},\tfrac{a}{t},\tfrac{D}{t}\bigr)},&\quad\!\!\text{if $D$ and $b/t$ are even but $D/t$ is odd and $a$ is a multiple of $t$;
}\\[4.30554pt]
\sqrt{t\,}\cdot{\mathrm{e}}^{i\varphi\bigl(\tfrac{bh}{t},\tfrac{a}{t},\tfrac{D}{t}\bigr)},&\quad\!\!\text{if $D$ is odd, $h\equiv 2^{-1}\!\!\!\!\pmod{D}$, and $a$ is a multiple of $t$;
}\\[4.30554pt]
0\,,&\quad\!\!\text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.\mspace{-36mu}

In each case, if we let
t=\gcd(b,D)
, we have
\bigl\lvert\Gamma(a,b,D)\bigr\rvert=\sqrt{t\,}
if
a
is a multiple of
t
and the value of
{(D+\!\!\;Db/t^{2})}
is even, and
\Gamma(a,b,D)=0
otherwise.
In particular: for
b
a multiplicative unit modulo
D
(so that
t=1
), we have
\bigl\lvert\Gamma(a,b,D)\bigr\rvert=1
.
If furthermore we have
a=0
, we have
\Gamma(a,b,D)={\mathrm{e}}^{\pi i(D+1)k/4}
for some
k\in{\mathbb{Z}}
, from the formula for
\varphi(b,a,D)
given in Eqn. (
103b
).

Appendix D
Relationships between measures on
{\mathbf{D}}
, on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
, and on
{\mathbb{R}}

This Appendix consists of entirely supplemental observations, on the way in which discrete integrals over
{\mathbf{D}}
(or over
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
, considered as a topological group) may be related to measures over
{\mathbb{R}}
.
This motivates some preliminaries on discrete measures over
{\mathbb{R}}
, such as the Dirac delta.

D.1
Dirac deltas

When analysing functions on
{\mathbb{R}}
, it is not uncommon to consider a Dirac distribution
\delta
(also known as the ‘Dirac delta’), which is defined in such a way that for an interval
J\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}
,

\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in J}}f(x)\,\delta(x-a)\;\mathrm{d}x\;=\;\begin{cases}f(a),&\text{if $a\in J$};\\[2.15277pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(115)

One may conceive of
\delta(x)
as the limit of a family of formally definable functions, such as the Gaussians
\mathcal{N}_{1\!\!\;/n}(x)=\smash{\tfrac{n}{\sqrt{2}\pi}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-(nx)^{2}/2}}
as
n\to\infty
.
In principle, one may consider it as syntactic sugar for a measure
\mu_{\delta}
on
{\mathbb{R}}
, which for any interval
J\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}
satisfies
\mu(J)=1
if
0\in J
, and
\mu(J)=0
otherwise: we call this a ‘point-mass distribution’.
We may write
\delta_{a}(x)=\delta(x-a)
for any
a\in{\mathbb{R}}
, so that
\delta_{a}
describes a point-mass distribution at
a\in{\mathbb{R}}
: that is, a measure
\mu_{a}
such that
\mu_{a}(S)=1
if
a\in S
, and
\mu_{a}(S)=0
otherwise.
(More generally, a point-mass distribution is any distribution of the form
p_{a}\delta_{a}
for
p_{a}\neq 0
: the ‘mass’ of such a distribution is then
p_{a}
.)
The purpose of the Dirac distributions would then be to allow us to write
\,\int_{J}f(x)\,\delta_{a}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{J}f(x)\,\delta(x-a)\,\mathrm{d}x\,
in place of
\,\int_{J}f(x\!+\!a)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{a}\,
.
This provides a notational bridge between the discrete measures
\mu_{a}
and the more common (Lebesgue) measure, so that we may perform analysis as though consistently working with a single variety of integration.

D.2
Impulses and Dirac combs

A
discrete measure

\rho
on
{\mathbb{R}}
is a measure which is a linear combination of a countable (and possibly finite) number of such point-mass distributions.
While such measures are not real-valued functions on
{\mathbb{R}}
, we may say that
\rho(a)\neq 0
if for any function
f:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
, we have
\int_{(a\!\!\>-\!\!\>\varepsilon,a\!\!\>+\!\!\>\varepsilon)}f(x)\,\rho(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\longrightarrow\,p_{a}f(a)
for some
p_{a}\neq 0
, as
\varepsilon\to 0
.
We may refer to the contributions of the point-mass distributions as ‘impulses’: for a discrete measure
\rho
, we say that
\rho
has an impluse at
a
if
\rho(a)\neq 0
in this sense.

We define the
Dirac comb

\Sh
(see,
e.g.
, Ref.
[
48
]
) as a discrete distribution, consisting of a sequence of a sum of unit point-mass distributions on
{\mathbb{Z}}
:

\Sh(x)\,=\,\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\delta_{t}(x)\;.

(116)

The Dirac comb is its own Fourier transform, which allows us to also express it as:

\Sh(x)\,=\,\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi ikx}\,=\,\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi ikx}.

(117)

We may use the Dirac comb to express any function
\phi:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
as a complex linear combination of impulses at the integers: if we let
\phi^{\prime}:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
be any extension of
\phi
to the real numbers, we may define the complex-valued discrete ‘distribution’
\mathbf{I}\>\!\phi
on
{\mathbb{R}}
, by

\mathbf{I}\>\!\phi(x)\;=\;\Sh(x)\,\phi^{\prime}(x)\;=\;\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\delta_{t}(x)\,\phi(t).

(118)

This will allow us to express sums on integers, in terms of integrals over
{\mathbb{R}}
: for instance, for any integers
a<b
, we then have

\int\limits_{\mathclap{(a,b]}}\mathbf{I}\!\>\phi(x)\;\mathrm{d}x\;=\;\sum_{\mathclap{a<t\leqslant b}}\phi(t);

(119)

in particular, we have
\int_{(a,b]}\Sh(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=b-a
, which is the number of integers in the interval
(a,b]
.
Finally, we may consider normalised versions of the Dirac comb with impulses at integer multiples of any interval length
\ell>0
:

\Sh_{\ell}(x)\,=\,\ell\,\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\delta_{\ell t}(x)\,=\,\ell\,\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\delta(x-\ell t)\,=\,\ell\,\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{2\pi ikx/\ell}.

(120)

The leading scalar factor of
\ell
in these sums, ensures that for
a<b
which are integer multiples of
\ell
, we again have
\int_{(a,b]}\Sh(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=b-a
.
We may then use this to define a generalisation of
\mathbf{I}
, to embed functions
\phi:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
as complex-valued measures in
{\mathbb{R}}
, but with impulses at intervals of
\ell>0
: for
\phi^{\prime}
again any extension of
\phi
to
{\mathbb{R}}
, we define

\mathbf{I}_{\ell}\;\!\phi(x)\;=\;\Sh_{\ell}(x)\,\phi^{\prime}(\tfrac{1}{\ell}x)\;=\;\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\delta_{\ell t}(x)\,\phi(t).

(121)

D.3
Motivating measures for
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
via continuous groups

In principle, the analysis of Section
3.1
, on measures on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
and constraints on them motivated by the Fourier transform, stands on its own.
However, the reader may be interested in certain observations of how consistent this is with Fourier analysis on
{\mathbb{R}}
, or whether our observations of measure could be motivated with reference to continuous cyclic groups.

We discuss how this may be done below, by considering how we may model functions
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
in terms of complex-valued discrete distributions with period
N
.
This will require some further preliminaries, in particular on the subject of discrete distributions on
{\mathbb{R}}
.

D.3.1
Elementary number theory and periodic functions on
{\mathbb{Z}}

We begin with some supplemental background on arithmetic modulo
D
, using this as a framework to consider periodic functions
f:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
.

Elements of
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
are often represented by integers drawn from the set of integers
0\leqslant x<D
, though we may represent them by the set of integers
{\mathbf{D}}:=\{L,L\,{+}\,1,\ldots,U\,{-}\,1,U\}
for any integers such that
U-L+1=D
.
(In this Appendix, we adopt a convention of
L=-\lfloor\tfrac{1}{2}(D-1)\rfloor
and
U=\lceil\tfrac{1}{2}(D-1)\rceil
, to simplify a certain description of a relartionship with
{\mathbb{R}}
.)
On may construct
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
as a set of equivalence classes of integers which differ by multiples of
D
,

x+D{\mathbb{Z}}\,=\,\bigl\{x+nD\,\big|\,n\in{\mathbb{Z}}\bigr\},

(122)

equipped with addition
{(x\!\!\>+\!\!\>D{\mathbb{Z}})+(y\!\!\>+\!\!\>D{\mathbb{Z}})}={(x\!\!\>+\!\!\>y)+D{\mathbb{Z}}}
and multiplication
{(x\!\!\>+\!\!\>D{\mathbb{Z}})\!\!\>\cdot\!\!\>(y\!\!\>+\!\!\>D{\mathbb{Z}})}={(xy)+D{\mathbb{Z}}}
.
Representatives
x\in{\mathbf{D}}
then serve as short-hand for the corresponding equivalence class
x+D{\mathbb{Z}}
.
(We may occasionally conflate
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
with such sets of representatives.)

There is a ring homomorphism
\pi_{D}:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
(the ‘canonical projection’) which may be defined by
\pi_{D}(x)=x+D{\mathbb{Z}}
.
We may use this to define a transformation
\mathbf{L}
on functions, which carries maps
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
to periodic functions
\mathbf{L}f:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
, given by
\mathbf{L}f=f\circ\pi_{D}
.
Then
\mathbf{L}
‘lifts’ functions
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
to functions
\mathbf{L}f
, which are ‘well-defined’ modulo
D
in the sense that
\mathbf{L}f(x)=\mathbf{L}f(x+nD)
for any
n\in{\mathbb{Z}}
.
By an abuse of notation, for any integer
x\in{\mathbf{D}}
, we may write
\mathbf{L}f(x)=f(x)
.

D.3.2
Constructing continuous cyclic groups from
{\mathbb{R}}

In order to consider Fourier analysis over
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
in terms of discrete integrals, in which the measure
N=\mu({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})
may be a parameter which we do not assign a value in advance, it will be helpful to relate functions
f:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
with period
D
, to functions
g:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
with period
N
.
We use this to consider a measure on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
in terms of a measure on a compact continuous group.

We define an additive group of real numbers modulo
N
, for any
N>1
, consisting of equivalence classes of real numbers which differ by multiples of
N
:

z+N{\mathbb{Z}}\,=\,\bigl\{z+tN\,\big|\,t\in{\mathbb{Z}}\bigr\},

(123)

equipped with addition
{(y\!\!\>+\!\!\>N{\mathbb{Z}})+(z\!\!\>+\!\!\>N{\mathbb{Z}})}={(y\!\!\>+\!\!\>z)+N{\mathbb{Z}}}
.
Just as we may represent
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
by representative integers
x\in{\mathbf{D}}={(-\tfrac{1}{2}D,\tfrac{1}{2}D]\!\>\cap\!\>{\mathbb{Z}}}
, we adopt the convention of representing
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
by an interval
J_{N}=(-\tfrac{1}{2}N,\tfrac{1}{2}N]
of representatives.
We may then think of
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
in terms of the interval
J_{N}
, with ‘wrap-around’ boundary conditions for addition and subtraction when the result of normal addition over
{\mathbb{R}}
yields a result which lies outside of
J_{N}
.
Note that we may regard
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
as a topological group, and one with a measure
\mu_{N}
inherited from the real numbers, consisting of the restriction of the Lebesgue measure to the interval
J_{N}
: in particular, we have
\mu_{N}({\mathbb{R}}_{N})=N
.

Finally, for a fixed integer
D>1
, note that we may define an injection
j_{N}:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
from the additive group
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
to the group
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
, by simply taking

j_{N}\bigl(x+D{\mathbb{Z}}\bigr)\;=\;\tfrac{N}{D}\bigl(x+D{\mathbb{Z}}\bigr)\;=\;\tfrac{N}{D}x+N{\mathbb{Z}}

(124)

for
x\in{\mathbb{Z}}
; we may abuse notation to describe this more concisely by writing
j_{N}(x)=\tfrac{N}{D}x
for
x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
.

D.3.3
Interpretation of measures on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
in terms of measures on
{\mathbb{R}}

To consider a notion of measure for
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
in terms of a continuous group, we may consider the injection
j_{N}:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
for some
N>0
.
This motivates considering how we may represent functions
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
in terms of ‘complex valued discrete measures’
\phi:{\mathbb{R}}_{N}\to{\mathbb{C}}
, which we may integrate over
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
to assign a meaning to an integral of
f
over
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
.

We do this by considering the related concept of periodic functions on
{\mathbb{Z}}
, and their representation by periodic discrete measures on
{\mathbb{R}}
.
Following Section
D.3.1
, we may ‘lift’ any
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
to a periodic function
\mathbf{L}f:{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\mathbb{C}}
with period
D
.
We may then represent
\mathbf{L}f
as a complex-valued discrete distribution, with impulses at invervals of length
\ell=N/D
, by acting on it with the transform
\mathbf{I}_{\ell}=\mathbf{I}_{N\!\!\>/\!\!\>D}

as defined in Eqn. (
121
).
Define the composite operator
\mathbf{E}_{N}=\mathbf{I}_{N\!\!\>/\!\!\>D\;\!}\mathbf{L}
, so that

\mathbf{E}_{N}f(z)\,=\,\ell\,\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\delta_{t\ell}(z)\,\mathbf{L}f(t)\,=\,\frac{N}{D}\,\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\>\!\delta_{tN\!\!\>/\!\!\>D}(z)\;\mathbf{L}f(t).

(125)

In particular, representing elements of
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
by
x\in{\mathbf{D}}
, the values of
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
at each
x
is represented by an impulse at
\tfrac{N}{D}x\in(-\tfrac{1}{2}N,\tfrac{1}{2}N]=J_{N}
, and also at
\tfrac{N}{D}(x+tD)=\tfrac{N}{D}x+tN
for each integer
t\in{\mathbb{Z}}
.
Then
\mathbf{E}_{N}f
is a discrete distribution with period
N
, which can be characterised in terms of its behaviour on the interval
J_{N}
.
In particular,

\int\limits_{J_{N}}\!\mathrm{d}z\;\mathbf{E}_{N}f(z)\;=\;\frac{N}{D}\int\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}_{N}}\!\mathrm{d}z\;\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\delta_{t\ell}(z)\,\mathbf{L}f(t)\;=\;\frac{N}{D}\sum_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in{\mathbf{D}}\end{subarray}}}\,\mathbf{L}f(t)\;=\;\frac{N}{D}\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}f(t)\;=\;\int\limits_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}}f(x)\;\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\,.

(126)

The fact that
\mu({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})=N
then reflects the choice of the period
N
(or equivalently: the modulus
N
) for the injection
j_{N}:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
, and that as a discretisation of the measure
\mu_{N}
on
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
(derived from the Lebesgue measure), we have
\mu({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})=\mu_{N}({\mathbb{R}}_{N})=N
.
In some sense, one may regard the injection
j_{N}
as describing a way that
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
represents a discretisation of the continuous group
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
, by condensing the usual measure of
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
at a discrete set of points at intervals of
\tfrac{N}{D}
.

D.3.4
Relating the Fourier transform on
{\mathbb{R}}
to measures on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}

The representation of the Fourier transform in Section
3.2
can be interpreted, as arising from how the Fourier transform on
{\mathbb{R}}
affects the discrete measures
\mathbf{E}_{N}f
arising from functions
f:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
.
In particular: the Fourier transform will generally transform such distributions, to other distributions which may be regarded as being defined with respect to a different measure.
Consider the Fourier transform
\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}
:

\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}(y)\;=\;\int\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}}\mathrm{d}z\;\mathbf{E}_{N}f(z)\;{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi iyz}\,:

(127)

substituting in the expression for
\widehat{f}_{N}
in Eqn. (
125
), we obtain

\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}(y)\;

\displaystyle=\;\frac{N}{D}\int\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}}\mathrm{d}z\;\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\delta_{tN\!\!\>/\!\!\>D}(z)\,\mathbf{L}f(t)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi iyz}\;=\;\frac{N}{D}\sum_{t\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\mathbf{L}f(t)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi iy(tN\!\!\>/\!\!\>D)}\;.

(128)

Separating the summation index
t\in{\mathbb{Z}}
into representatives of
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
and shifts by an entire period, we may then write

\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}(y)\;

\displaystyle=\;\frac{N}{D}\mathop{\sum\sum}_{\mathclap{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in{\mathbf{D}},\tau\in{\mathbb{Z}}\end{subarray}}}\,\mathbf{L}f(x)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi iyN\!\!\;(x+\tau\!\!\>D)\!\!\;/\!\!\;D}\;=\;\frac{N}{D}\sum_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}}\,f(x)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi iyNx/D}\biggl[\,\sum_{\tau\in{\mathbb{Z}}}{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi i\tau yN}\biggr],

(129)

factorising away the dependence on
\tau
in square brackets.
By Eqn. (
120
), that bracketed expression is in fact
\tfrac{1}{N}\Sh_{N}(y)
: rewriting this as a sum of impulses, we then have

\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}(y)

\displaystyle=\,\frac{N}{D}\sum_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}}\,f(x)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi iyNx/D}\biggl[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\delta_{k\!\!\;/\!\!\>N}(y)\biggr]\;=\;\frac{1}{D}\mathop{\sum\sum}_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\!\!\;D}\!\!\;,\!\>k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}}\,\delta_{k\!\!\;/\!\!\>N}(y)\,f(x)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi ikx/D}\,.

(130)

That is,
\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}
is itself a complex discrete measure, which is zero for any
y
which is not an integer multiple of
\tfrac{1}{N}
.
By construction, it repeats after every
D
impulses, and so has a period of
D/N
.
Then
\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}=\mathbf{E}_{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{$\scriptstyle D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N$}}g
for a function
g:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{C}}
,

\mathbf{E}_{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{$\scriptstyle D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N$}}g(y)\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,\delta_{k\!\!\;/\!\!\>N}(y)\,\mathbf{L}g(k),

(131)

which we can see holds for

g(k)\;=\;\frac{N}{D}\sum_{\mathclap{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}}}\,f(x)\;{\mathrm{e}}^{-2\pi ikx/D}\;=\;\hat{f}(k),

(132)

for
\hat{f}
as defined by Eqn. (
20
), with the integral over
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
explicitly expanded as a sum using Eqn. (
13
) and using the measure
\mu
such that
\mu({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})=N
.

This demonstrates that
\widehat{\mathbf{E}_{N}f}=\smash{\mathbf{E}_{D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N}\hat{f}}
, subject to this representation of the Fourier transform over
{\mathbb{R}}
.
However,
\smash{\mathbf{E}_{D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N}\hat{f}}
is a complex-valued discrete measure which has period
D/N
, and where in particular a representative interval would be
J_{D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N}
.
This suggests that
\hat{f}
should be interpreted in terms of the group injection
j_{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{$\scriptstyle D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N$}}:{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N}
, which would motivate a measure
\mu^{\prime}
on
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
such that
\mu^{\prime}({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})=\mu_{\raisebox{-0.75346pt}{$\scriptstyle D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N$}}({\mathbb{R}}_{D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N})=D/N
.

In summary: if we take
f:({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu)\to{\mathbb{C}}
as a function on the measure space
({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu)
with
\mu({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})=N
, we effectively interpret
f
in terms of a measure on the topological space
{\mathbb{R}}_{N}
, which has a total measure of
N
.
The Fourier transform
\hat{f}
is then most appropriately regarded as a measure on the topological space
{\mathbb{R}}_{D\!\!\>/\!\!\>N}
, which has a total measure of
D/N
, so that
\hat{f}:({\mathbb{Z}}_{D},\mu^{\prime})\to{\mathbb{C}}
, where
\mu^{\prime}({\mathbb{Z}}_{D})=D/N
.
If we wish for
\mu=\mu^{\prime}
, so that
f
and
\smash{\hat{f}}
have the same domain when we consider
{\mathbb{Z}}_{D}
as a measure space, we must take
N=\sqrt{D}
, in agreement with the results of Section
3.2
.
